title: Frequency arrays
overview: So far an array index has only been a position: `a[0]` is the first number, `a[1]` the second. Module 13 adds one new idea: use the **number itself as the index**. Make a counting array `f` filled with zeros. Whenever you read a number `x`, do `f[x]++`. After one loop, `f[x]` tells you how many times `x` appeared, with no searching. This is called a frequency array.

concepts.explain: From the earlier modules you can read `n` numbers into an array with a loop, reach any element with `a[i]`, and count things with `cnt++`. Module 13 puts these together in a new way.

concepts.term: The new idea: the value is the index
concepts.explain: Until now you asked "which number is at position `i`?". A frequency array asks the other way round: "how many times did the number `x` show up?". The answer is kept in slot `f[x]`.

Input `1 2 3 4 5 3 2 1 5 3`. Start with `f` all zeros. Each number adds 1 to its own slot. At the end `f[1] = 2`, `f[2] = 2`, `f[3] = 3`, `f[4] = 1` and `f[5] = 2`. Print `f[1]` to `f[5]` and you have the answer.

concepts.term: Why not count with two loops?
concepts.explain: You could: for each `i` from 1 to M, walk the whole array and count the `i`s. But with N and M up to 100000 that is about 10^10 steps, far too slow for 1 second. The frequency array walks the numbers only once.
Every slot must start at 0 before you count. Inside `main`, write `int f[100005] = {0};`. An array declared above `main` (a global array) starts at zero on its own.
The biggest number you may see must still be a valid index. If numbers go up to 100000, `f[100000]` must exist, so declare at least 100001 slots.
Sometimes you only need to know whether `x` appeared. Then write `f[x] = 1` instead of `f[x]++`.
In Module 11, `c - '0'` turned a digit character into its value. In the same way `ch - 'a'` turns `a`..`z` into 0..25, so 26 slots can count lowercase letters.

files.title: Presence array with yes/no queries
files.what: Marks which numbers are in the array, prints the marks for 0 to 9, then answers queries asking whether a number is present.
steps: For each `a[i]`, set `freq[a[i]] = 1` to mark it as present.
Print `i` and `freq[i]` for `i` from 0 to 9, so you can see the marks.
Read `m` queries. For each `x`, print `YES` if `freq[x] == 1`, otherwise `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(max value)
files.output_note: The first 10 lines are `value mark`. Only 2, 3, 4 and 7 show `1`, and the repeated 4 is still just `1`. Then come the answers `4 YES`, `5 NO` and `7 YES`.
files.watch_out: A value of 100000 or more would write past the end of `freq`. Always check the limits before choosing the array size.

check.q: Why does 4 show 1 and not 2, even though it appears twice?
check.a: The code sets `freq[x] = 1` instead of adding 1, so it only records presence.

files.title: Frequency Array (count 1..M)
files.what: Counts how many times each number from 1 to M appears. This is the counting version of the frequency array.
steps: `int f[100000];` is global, so every slot starts at 0.
Read each number and do `f[a[i]] += 1` in the same loop.
Print `f[1]`, `f[2]`, and so on up to `f[m]`, one per line.
files.input_note: The sample from the statement: N = 10 numbers, each between 1 and M = 5.
files.output_note: Line i is how many times i appears: `2` (two 1s), `2` (two 2s), `3` (three 3s), `1` (one 4) and `2` (two 5s). This matches the expected output in the statement.
files.watch_out: The array `a` isn't really needed. You could read into a temporary `x` and do `f[x]++`.

check.q: If M were 6 with the same numbers, what would line 6 show?
check.a: `0`, because 6 never appears and a global array starts at zero.

files.title: Distinct letters in a string
files.what: Finds which lowercase letters appear in a fixed string and how many different letters there are. It uses a 26-slot presence array.
steps: The string is hard-coded as `"aaaaaagggggccjcc"`, and `f[26]` starts at zeros.
For each character, `ch - 'a'` gives its slot, and that slot is set to 1.
Loop over the 26 slots. Add each `f[i]` to `cnt`, and if `f[i]` is 1, print the letter `i + 'a'`.
Print `cnt`, the number of different letters.
files.output_note: `a 1`, `c 1`, `g 1` and `j 1` come out in alphabetical order, even though `g` comes before `c` in the string. The last line is `4`.
files.watch_out: Only lowercase letters are safe. An uppercase letter or a digit would give a negative index or one above 25.

check.q: Why do the letters come out sorted?
check.a: The second loop goes through the slots in order from 0 (`a`) to 25 (`z`), not in string order.

recap: A frequency array uses the number as the index: `f[x]` is about the number `x`.
`f[x]++` counts. `f[x] = 1` only marks that `x` was seen.
Fill it with zeros first, and make it bigger than the largest possible number.
One pass over the input is enough. There is no need to search the array again and again.
`ch - 'a'` turns a lowercase letter into an index from 0 to 25.
Printing `f` from the small end to the big end lists the values in sorted order.

check_yourself.q: After counting `2, 4, 3, 4, 5` into `freq`, what are `freq[4]` and `freq[0]`?
In a letter-count array, which letter does index 7 belong to?
When is a frequency array a bad idea?
check_yourself.a: When values can be huge (for example up to 10^9) or negative. The array would be too big, or the index would be invalid.
